title: Effect of recrystallization on bainite transformation and mechanical properties of complex phase steel with high formability (CH steel)
abstract:
Herein, the effect of recrystallization on the bainite transformation and mechanical properties of CH steel were investigated using SEM, TEM, EBSD, dilatometry, and tensile testing machine. First, precipitation was introduced to hinder recrystallization by batch annealing. Subsequently, the competitive relationship between austenite transformation and recrystallization was revealed using different annealing processes. Finally, the effect of recrystallization on bainite transformation was analyzed, mainly including bainite morphology, fraction, transformation rate, bainite nucleation rate of untransformed austenite and austenite-bainite orientation relationship, as well as the effect on the mechanical properties. After batch annealing, a large amount of cementite and nanoscale (Nb, Ti)C precipitated in the hot-rolled sheet, the austenite transformation start temperature (A
                     c1) and the pearlite to austenite transformation end temperature (A
                     c1f)of the cold-rolled sheet increased, and the austenite transformation end temperature (A
                     c3) of the cold-rolled sheet decreased, and the austenite transformation process accelerated. The microstructure of annealed sheets is consisted of ferrite, granular bainite, martensite, and a small fraction of retained austenite. Carbide hindered the recrystallization process during the annealing process, resulting in significant refining of the grains. The lower degree of recrystallization promoted bainite transformation, providing more nucleation sites, higher grain boundary and autocatalytic nucleation activation energy, improving bainite's fraction and transformation rate. The bainitic ferrite was mainly lathy in the recrystallized zone and polygonal in the non-recrystallized zone. Both a K-S and an N-W relationship between retained austenite and bainite, while the N-W relationship in the non-recrystallized zone was relatively higher. Without severe loss of plasticity, hindering recrystallization increased the dislocation, grain refinement, and precipitation strengthening values of the samples, and the strength significantly improved. However, with the increase of annealing temperature, recrystallization fraction increased gradually, and the increase in strength became less noticeable.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: The number of cars per capita keeps rising as the economy becomes better, which creates issues like excessive fuel use and environmental pollution. People now need to find solutions to these issues. According to research results, if the car body weight is reduced by 10%, the fuel consumption can be reduced by 5.5%, thereby reducing emissions [ 1 , 2 ]. Therefore, automobile lightweight, as one of the most effective measures to reduce energy consumption and emissions, urgently needs the development of high strength and high formability automotive steels [ 3 ]. In recent years, the concept of complex phase steel with high formability (CH) steel was proposed in standard VDA 239-100. Compared with the complex phase steel (CP) steel, the CH steel has a uniform and finer microstructures and a small amount of retained austenite, so the formability is significantly improved. The chemical composition of CH steel is slightly adjusted on the basis of CP steel. Increasing the content of Si + Al to introduce a small amount of retained austenite to exert an appropriate transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect, adding microalloying elements such as Nb and Ti to introduce the second phase to exert precipitation strengthening and grain strengthening, which will not make substantial adjustments to the production process due to changes in the chemical composition, thereby increasing the manufacturing cost of the product. The microstructure of CH steel is generally composed of three or more of ferrite, bainite, martensite and retained austenite, with fine and uniform microstructure and good formability, which can be used to manufacture various types of parts with high requirements for local formability [ 4 ]. Compared to high-strength steels, such as dual phase (DP) steel, dual phase with high formability (DH) steel and TRIP steel, CH steel has higher yield strengths, hole-expanding ratio and bending properties [ 5 , 6 ]. Together with the simple manufacturing process and meeting the high-performance requirements, it is foreseeable that CH steel will be more widely used in automotive steel.

To further improve the strength of automotive steel, under the condition of not changing the composition, the methods adopted by steel research scholars mainly include: (1) increasing the heating rate to delay recrystallization, refine the grain and increase the strength [ 7–9 ]; (2) using cyclic pre-quenching to prepare a uniform lamellar microstructure, which improves the strength and plasticity simultaneously [ 10–12 ]; (3) combing of the precipitation strengthening and grain refinement strengthening of the precipitates improves the strength and the balance of the strength-plasticity [ 13 ]. By increasing the heating rate of TRIP steel from 3  ° C/s to 500  ° C/s, Xu et al. [ 7 ] delayed the recrystallization to above the starting temperature of austenite transformation, causing the grains to be refined, and the tensile strength improved from 950.4 MPa to 1035.2 MPa, while the total elongation decreased from 22.1% to 17.9%. Ding et al. [ 11 ] obtained a dual phase steel with uniform microstructure distribution and lamellar morphology through three-time cyclic quenching. Excellent deformation compatibility between lamellar martensite and lamellar ferrite increases strength and plasticity. Mohrbacher et al. [ 13 ] performed a batch annealing treatment on the hot-rolled sheet before cold rolling to promote precipitation. During the annealing process, recrystallization and grain coarsening were inhibited, and precipitation and grain refinement strengthening worked simultaneously. The strength is increased by 180 MPa, which satisfies the performance requirements of DH980 very well. In conclusion, method (2) has a cumbersome procedure that raises the cost and reduces the output. Methods (1) and (3) increase the strength by adjusting the relationship between recrystallization and austenite transformation. However, method (1) has been studied in various steels, and the method (3) is rarely explored. In addition, the process of method (3) is the simplest and most feasible for the industrial production of CH steel. Therefore, it is necessary to explore the effect of recrystallization on the microstructure and properties of CH steel by method (3) to provide a basis for the industrial production of CH steel.

Previous literatures only studied the effect of recrystallization on austenite transformation during critical annealing [ 14–16 ]. The degree of recrystallization will affect the nucleation position, morphology and fraction of austenite, and the newly formed austenite will further hinder the recrystallization process. The substructure in the incompletely recrystallized sample is used to provide more nucleation points for austenite to promote austenite transformation and refine the structure, and the strength improves, which is reflected in the mechanical properties. Common ways to hinder the recrystallization include rapid heating, and the solute drag effect and the pinning effect of fine precipitates by adding microalloying elements [ 17–20 ]. For multiphase steels, the influence of the competitive relationship between recrystallization and austenite transformation during annealing will continue to the subsequent isothermal and secondary quenching processes. Austenite transforms into bainite during the isothermal process, and part of the austenite transforms into martensite after quenching to room temperature while the rest of it remains at room temperature. However, the effect of the relationship between recrystallization and austenite transformation during annealing on the later transformation evolution is less studied, especially the effect on the bainite transformation of the main microstructure in CH steel. Previous studies on the influence of bainite transformation mainly concentrated on elements [ 21–23 ], prior austenitic grain size [ 24 , 25 ], isothermal temperature [ 26 , 27 ], annealing temperature, precipitation [ 28 , 29 ], and deformation [ 30 ]. Herein, based on the actual production process, the introduction of precipitates through batch annealing to hinder recrystallization and the effect of recrystallization on the microstructure and properties of CH steel was revealed, especially the effect of recrystallization on bainite transformation, providing a theoretical basis for the industrial production of CH steel and helping to achieve the low-carbon target.

sections.heading: Materials and heat treatment
paragraphs:
In the present study, test steels for all processes were prepared in the laboratory. The chemical composition of the ingot is shown in  Table 1 
                         . The austenite transformation starting temperature and the austenite transformation finishing temperature of the ingot were tested by the Bähr D805L dilatometry, which was 704 °C and 972 °C, respectively. A 3.8 mm hot-rolled sheet was obtained by vacuum induction melting, forging, and hot rolling. The hot rolling start temperature was 1150 °C, and the final rolling temperature was 890 °C. Laminar cooling was used to cool to 550 °C to simulate coiling. After holding for 60 min, it was cooled to room temperature with the furnace. The hot-rolled sheet is marked as HR steel. In order to delay recrystallization to introduce more precipitates, the hot-rolled sheet was kept in a batch annealing furnace (KSL-1100X–S) at 580 °C for 12 h and cooled to room temperature in air, marked as HR-t steel. The batch annealing temperature should be selected as high as possible while being lower than the maximum cementite precipitation temperature and austenite transformation start temperature. The HR steel and HR-t steel were processed to cold rolling after pickling in 36∼38 vol% hydrochloric acid, and the thickness of the cold-rolled sheet was approximately 1.8 mm with an about 53% thickness reduction. The cold-rolled sheets corresponding to the two hot-rolled sheets are marked as CR steel and CR-t steel, respectively.

In order to provide a reference for the continuous annealing process, the austenite transformation of CR and CR-t steels during continuous heating was analyzed in detail using a dilatometer. The thermal expansion curves and their first-order derivatives of CR and CR-t steel during continuous heating to 1200 °C at a heating rate of 10 C/s are shown in  Fig. 1 
                         , along with some key nodes on the derivative curves. The austenite transformation start temperature ( A 
                         c1 ), the pearlite to austenite transformation end temperature ( A 
                         c1f ) and the austenite transformation end temperature ( A 
                         c3 ) are determined. The recrystallization start temperature is described as points A and a, the austenite formation start temperature is described as points B, b, the peak temperature of the pearlite to austenite transformation is described as points C and c, the end temperature of the pearlite to austenite transformation is described as points D and d (it is lower than the end temperature of pearlite to austenite transformation, which explanation has been found in the literature [ 31 ]), the peak temperature of the transformation of the ferrite to austenite transformation is described as points E and e, and the end temperature of austenite formation is described as point F and f. Before  A 
                         c1 , the decline of the derivative curves in the AB and ab intervals was mainly caused by recrystallization [ 32 ], and the recrystallization start temperature of CR and CR-t was similar, but obviously, the decline of the derivative curves of CR-t was lower than that of CR, meaning the recrystallization degree of CR-t is lower than that of CR before austenite transformation.  A 
                         c1 、 A 
                         c1f  of CR-t are higher than CR, but the peak temperature of the ferrite to austenite transformation and  A 
                         c3  of CR-t are lower than those of CR. It can be concluded that the process of austenite transformation is accelerated, and the intercritical temperature range is narrowed.

Heat treatments were performed on a continuous annealing simulator (CCT-AY-II produced by Ulvac-Riko INC., Japan), and the cooling medium was nitrogen. The cold-rolled sheet was heated to 780 °C, 820 °C, 860 °C and 880 °C at a heating rate of 10 °C/s for 10 s and 90 s, respectively, to obtain different contents of ferrite and austenite, then cooled to 380 °C at a cooling rate of 45  ° C/s for 600 s to support the bainite transformation fully, and finally cooled to room temperature at a cooling rate of 10 °C/s. The whole process schematic diagram and test steel nomenclature notes are shown in  Fig. 2 
                          and  Table 2 
                         . In comparison to CH steel, the CH-t steel goes through an extra batch annealing step during preparation. In addition, the austenite fraction during the intercritical annealing process was measured by cooling to room temperature at a cooling rate of 45 °C/s directly after the intercritical annealing.

sections.heading: Microstructure of hot-rolled sheet
paragraphs:
The microstructure of the hot-rolled sheet both before and after the batch annealing is shown in  Fig. 3 
                            . The microstructure of HR steel is granular bainite (GB) with very little (Nb, Ti)C, and the precipitates will be characterized in 3.3.1. In HR-t steel, the martensite/austenite islands (M/A islands) decomposed, a significant quantity of cementite and (Nb, Ti)C were precipitated, the grain boundaries were blurred, bainite laths merged, and the fraction of low angle grain boundaries decreased [ 36 ]. Differences in the microstructure that exist now can be heritable to microstructural and carbide evolution during continuous annealing. At the same time, the hardness of HR steel and HR-t steel were measured. HR steel had a hardness of 334.8 HV, whereas HR-t steel had a hardness of 300.0 HV, a 10.4% reduction in hardness.

sections.heading: Microstructures of cold-rolled steel
paragraphs:
The microstructures of the two hot-rolled sheets after being cold-rolled to 1.8 mm are shown in  Fig. 4 
                            . The bainitic ferrite (BF) of CR steel is almost parallel to the rolling direction, especially the substructure in GB is arranged along the rolling direction. No deformation was found in the M/A islands, the small size M/A islands were arranged along the rolling direction, and the big size M/A islands were almost unchanged. The overall shape of CR-t steel is fibrous along the rolling direction, which is related to the softening that occurs after batch annealing. Carbides composed of cementite and precipitates are evenly distributed, and a small quantity of tempered M/A has not deformed despite tempering. It can be concluded that the M/A island plays the role of the hard phase of GB, and the large-sized M/A is difficult to coordinate deformation, which is quite different from the deformation ability of bainitic ferrite. After being cold-rolled at the same reduction ratio, the cold-rolled distortion energy of CR steel is greater, which also provides a higher driving force for recrystallization and austenite transformation during annealing [ 37 ].

sections.heading: Microstructures of annealed sheet
paragraphs:
The microstructures of the annealed sheets treated by different processes are shown in  Figs. 5 and 6 
                            
                            . The microstructures are all composed of ferrite (F), granular bainite, martensite (M), and a small amount of retained austenite (RA). With the increase of annealing temperature and prolongation of annealing time, the fraction of bands of non-recrystallized ferrite (NF) and the fraction of recrystallized polygonal ferrite (PF) gradually decrease, the fraction of granular bainite increases progressively, and the distribution of martensite blocks gets uniform. The recrystallization process of the CH-t steel is significantly delayed. When the annealing time is 10 s, the annealing time is short, and the grains are refined. There are undissolved cementite and small M/A islands in the low-temperature annealing steels, and the body matrix looks very messy. As the annealing temperature is extended to 90 s, the amount of austenite transformation increases, the size of each phase increases significantly, the cementite dissolves, and the bainitic ferrite and ferrite matrix appear to be clean. There are two types of GB formed in the isothermal process: one is composed of polygonal BF and diffuse M/A islands, while the other is composed of lathy BF and M/A islands with certain orientations [ 26 , 38 ]. As the temperature increases and the time prolongs, the bainitic ferrite gradually appears as a lath structure. The proportion of the first type of GB in CH-t steel is larger than that of CH steel. The GB of CH steel is generally uniformly distributed. However, the GB of CH-t steel is not only uniformly distributed but also banded, and the fraction of GB is relatively high. Therefore, it is speculated that banded bainite is transformed from non-recrystallized banded austenite. It is clear that the austenite transformation and recrystallization in the annealing process have a great influence on the morphology, distribution, and size of the intermediate-temperature product bainite and low-temperature product martensite after subsequent cooling, which we will explore in detail in  4.1  and  4.2.

Fig. 7 
                             shows the EBSD results of CR and CR-t steel annealed at 780 °C and 860 °C for 10 s and 90 s. The IQ and grain boundary distribution map indicates the 2–5°, 5–15°, and 15–180° grain boundary by red lines, green lines, and blue lines, respectively. Generally, grain boundaries with an orientation greater than 15° are considered high angle grain boundaries. Otherwise, they are considered low angle grain boundaries, composed of dislocations and sub-grain boundaries. The recrystallized ferrite in white is polygonal and has a higher IQ value. The black area with a lower IQ value is carbon-rich martensite (CRM) with a higher dislocation density [ 39 ], and the gray area with IQ value between the white and black area is ferrite with higher strain or bainite. The high angle grain boundaries are mainly found on the grain boundaries between the recrystallized microstructures, especially in the samples with a higher degree of recrystallization, as shown in  Fig. 7 (a), (e), (i) , and (m). The low angle grain boundaries are mainly distributed in the non-recrystallized ferrite, the banded structure, and CRM, especially in samples with a lower degree of recrystallization, such as  Fig. 7 (c), (g), (k) , (o) shown. The misorientation angle proportion and body-centered cubic (BCC) phase average grain size are counted, as shown in  Table 3 
                            . The average grain size is the statistical result of grain equivalent circle diameter weighted by number. With the increase of annealing temperature and the prolongation of annealing time, the proportion of low angle grain boundaries is trending to decrease, and that of high angle grain boundaries is trending upward, and the degree of recrystallization is gradually increasing of CH-t steel. There is little change in the proportion of low and high angle grain boundaries in CH steel, proving that it has almost completely recrystallized after annealing at 780 °C for 10 s. The grain orientation of CH steel is relatively random, and CH-t steel always has prominent γ fiber (ND//<111>) and α fiber (RD//<110>) orientation. Additionally, it is found that the grain size of the BCC phase gradually increases with the increase of annealing temperature and prolongation of annealing time. The grain size of CH-t steel is significantly smaller than CH steel under the same process, which is the effect of austenite transformation preceding the recrystallization process. When the annealing time is 10 s, the grain refinement ranges from 9.5% to 24.6%. The difference between CH steel and CH-t steel gradually decreases when the annealing time is 90 s, and the grain refinement ranges from 6.8% to 13.3%.

sections.heading: Mechanical properties of hot-rolled sheet
paragraphs:
The mechanical properties of the hot-rolled sheet before and after batch annealing are shown in  Fig. 8 
                            . After batch annealing, the yield strength increases, the tensile strength decreases, and the elongation is almost unchanged. A large amount of cementite and precipitates are precipitated when the hot-rolled sheet is annealed. The yield strength increases by 137 MPa as a result of the smaller cementite and precipitates having a strong inhibitory effect on the dislocation migration during the stretching process. The microstructure recovers, and the number of low angle grain boundaries decreases. At the same time, M/A island decomposed and softened, more carbon atoms precipitated and less in solution, and the tensile strength decreased by 171 MPa. The larger-size cementite provides crack nucleation and propagation paths, resulting in lower strength and lower elongation [ 40 ].

sections.heading: Mechanical properties of annealed sheet
paragraphs:
The mechanical properties of annealed sheets of CH and CH-t steel are shown in  Table 4 
                            . When the annealing temperature is lower and the annealing time is shorter, the mechanical properties of CH steel and CH-t steel treated by the same process are quite different. With the increase in annealing temperature, the tensile strength and yield strength of CH steel and CH-t steel both show a decreasing trend. The strength of sheets annealed at 780 °C and 820 °C are relatively comparable, as is the strength of sheets annealed at 860 °C and 880 °C. However, elongation shows different trends with process changes. When the annealing time is 10 s, the yield strength and tensile strength of CH-t steel are higher than that of CH steel when the annealing temperature is 780 °C, 820 °C, and 860 °C. The strength improvement effect of CH-t steel is no longer apparent once the annealing temperature reaches 880 °C. When the annealing time is 90 s, the effect of increasing the strength of CH-t steel is not apparent above 860 °C. We elaborate on the relationship between microstructure and mechanical properties in  4.3.

sections.heading: Carbide characteristics
paragraphs: Precipitates were introduced by batch annealing to hinder recrystallization, so the precipitates of hot-rolled sheets and continuously annealed sheets were characterized and analyzed.

sections.heading: Carbide of hot-rolled sheet
paragraphs:
The precipitates analysis of HR and HR-t steel is shown in  Fig. 9 
                            . In addition to the large size (Nb, Ti)C that is not dissolved during hot rolling and heating, HR steel has no precipitates during the subsequent rolling and coiling process. After batch annealing, recovery and decomposition of M/A island occurred, and a large amount of short rod-shaped and near-spherical cementite precipitated. At the same time, long-time annealing promoted the precipitation of a large amount of nanoscale (Nb, Ti)C. At higher temperatures, replacement elements with better migration and diffusion capabilities, such as Mn, Cr, and Mo, are continuously distributed into cementite [ 41 ].

sections.heading: Carbide of annealed sheet
paragraphs:
The carbide characterization of 780-10, 780-10-t, 860-10, and 860-10-t steel is shown in  Fig. 10 
                            . The carbides are mainly distributed in a diffuse manner, which are mainly divided into cementite and (Nb, Ti)C. The cementite in 780-10 and 780-10-t steels size ranges from 40 nm to 100 nm, mainly in round or oval shapes. There is more cementite in 780-10-t than in 780-10 steel due to incomplete austenitization and the precursor HR-t of 780-10-t steel containing a significant quantity of undissolved cementite, as shown in  Fig. 10 (a) and (e) .  Fig. 1  shows that the temperature at which cementite completely dissolves in CR-t steel is higher than it is in CR steel, which is consistent with the results of the carbide characterization. Depending on size, (Nb, Ti)C can be divided into (Nb, Ti)C with a size larger than 100 nm and (Nb, Ti)C smaller than 50 nm. The (Nb, Ti)C with a size greater than 100 nm without dissolution exists in all samples [ 42 ]. The total solution temperature of (Nb, Ti)C was calculated to be 1262 °C in the earlier study [ 4 ]. (Nb, Ti)C with a size of less than 50 nm is mainly precipitated during the annealing process or grown from the fine precipitates in the precursor [ 26 ], and there are more in the high-temperature annealed samples 860-10 and 860-10-t steel, and 860-10-t contains more of the larger (Nb, Ti)C. To sum up, as the annealing temperature rises and the time prolongs, the cementite gradually dissolves, and the larger the size of (Nb, Ti)C, the greater the number of precipitates.

sections.heading: Recrystallization and austenite transformation during intercritical annealing
paragraphs:
In order to further characterize the competition between recrystallization and austenite transformation, we quantitatively analyzed the recrystallization and austenite transformation fraction of each sample, as shown in  Fig. 11 
                         . The fraction of austenite transformation was characterized by the SEM microstructure of the samples, which were directly quenched to room temperature after intercritical annealing. Bainite, martensite, and retained austenite are transformation products of intercritical austenite, and the austenite nucleation position was characterized by the EBSD results. The recrystallization fraction is characterized by the grain orientation spread (GOS) value, which is an important method to determine the area fraction of recrystallized grains [ 43 ]. The GOS indicates the average value of the difference between the average grain orientation and orientation of each nucleus in the grain. A smaller GOS indicates that the grain orientation gradient is lower, which means that the degree of lattice distortion is smaller [ 44 , 45 ]. In this paper, we used the GOS value ≤ 2° to characterize the recrystallization fraction of grains.

As shown in  Fig. 11 , the recrystallization fraction of CH steels was consistently higher than that of CH-t steels in any process, and it was higher in samples annealed for 90 s than in samples annealed for 10 s. The recrystallization of CH steels was essentially complete by the time they were annealed at 780 °C. However, the recrystallization of CH-t steels was significantly delayed. The recrystallization fraction of CH-t steels tended to increase with increasing temperature and annealing time. According to  Fig. 12 
                         , it was found that there were still non-recrystallized zones in the samples with small GOS values even after annealing at 860 °C/880 °C for 90 s. CH steels were mainly carbon-rich martensite aggregates and bainite/martensite zones with strain within the grain; there were also banded bainite zones in CH-t steels. These should have transformed from the non-recrystallized austenite, and the microstructure of CH-t demonstrated the importance of the microstructure heredity.

The austenite transformation mechanisms of CH and CH-t steels are different, and the distribution of RA is shown in  Fig. 13 
                         . The fraction and carbon content of retained austenite tested by XRD is marked in the upper right corner of the image. For CH steel, the formation of austenite begins after ferrite recrystallization ends, so austenite mainly nucleates on the recrystallized F/F, F and M/A islands grain boundaries, especially at the junction of the grain boundaries. Correspondingly, in CH steel, the RA is mainly distributed on the F/F, F/B, and F/M interfaces or junction of the grain boundaries, and a small part of RA is located on the bainite and martensite, where the bainite and martensite transformation does not occur after the isothermal process and secondary quenching. With the increase of annealing temperature, the grain size of RA gradually increases, and there is very little RA between the laths of bainite and martensite. For CH-t steel, carbides delay the recrystallization process, causing austenite transformation and recrystallization have a long overlapping process, as can be seen from  Figs. 1, 5 and 6 . At the cost of sacrificing recrystallization, the residual deformed substructure and surrounding carbides become preferential and effective nucleation sites for austenite [ 46 , 47 ], and the carbon diffusion distance for austenite growth becomes shorter, thereby refining austenite [ 48–50 ]. This phenomenon is also known as the “acceleration effect” of austenite transformation [ 51 , 52 ], and the “acceleration effect” is attributed to the defect structure and distortion energy in the deformed structure. Coupled with the pinning effect of (Nb, Ti)C, the grain refinement is more prominent. It is also important to note that the austenite in the <110> and <111> orientations nucleate preferentially in the non-recrystallized region. As the recrystallization fraction increases, the austenite nucleates in each orientation, which is shown in  Fig. 13 (c), (d), (g), and (h) .

As the annealing temperature increases, the recrystallization and austenite transformation fraction gradually increase, and the difference between CH steel and CH-t steel becomes less. When the annealing time is 90 s, as the annealing temperature increases, the austenite transformation of CH steel and CH-t steel increases approximately linearly, and the follows a similar trend, and the austenite fraction of CH-t steel is always higher than that of CH steel. When the annealing time is 10 s, the austenite transformation of the two steels differs significantly at lower temperatures, and the trend is similar at higher temperatures. The austenite fraction increases significantly between 820 °C and 860 °C when the annealing time is 10 s. It is speculated that the reason for the difference is the dissolution of cementite, which is consistent with the analysis results in  Fig. 1 . Compared with CH steel, the complete dissolution temperature of cementite in CH-t steel is higher. When the amount of undissolved cementite is large, there is not enough carbon for austenite transformation, coupled with the low distortion energy for CR-t steel, which reduces the nucleation and growth kinetics of austenite at the beginning [ 37 ]. The cementite is completely dissolved as the temperature increases and the time prolongs. Recrystallization retardation has a strong influence on promoting austenite transformation, and austenite transformation rate rises significantly.

sections.heading: Effect of recrystallization on bainite transformation
paragraphs:
We performed TEM characterization of the bainite in the recrystallization and non-recrystallization zones to explore the law of bainite transformation, as shown in  Fig. 14 
                         . The bainitic ferrite in 860-10 is mainly lathy structure, while the bainitic ferrite in 860-10-t steel is mainly polygonal, accompanied with high-density dislocations, and the size is obviously smaller, as shown in  Fig. 14 (a), (b), (d), and (e) . In contrast to BF with high-density dislocations, ferrite in 860-10-t steel is relatively clean, has lower dislocation density, and geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) only exists at the F/M boundary. In 860-10-t steel, a significant number of fine (Nb, Ti)C are evenly distributed. High-resolution TEM (HRTEM) characterization results show that (Nb,Ti)C has a low degree of lattice misfit with the α-Fe matrix, and has a Kurdjumov-Sachs (K-S) relationship with the α-Fe matrix. It is noted that (Nb, Ti)C with the lower lattice misfit with the matrix can be used as the nucleation point of bainite [ 53 ]. As the temperature increases and the time prolongs, the bainitic ferrite gradually appears a lathy structure. This rule can be seen from the comparison of the EBSD result  Fig. 13 . The morphology, size, and position of bainite are mainly affected by austenite, and the size and position of austenite are mainly affected by the competition between recrystallization and transformation. For CH steel, the recrystallization is basically completed before the austenite transformation, and the bainite is formed at the junction of three-grain boundaries, with a large size and a lathy shape. For CH-t steel, recrystallization and austenite transformation conduct simultaneously, and austenite will also form in the residual deformation substructure with a smaller size in a band. The smaller the austenite grains, the more nucleation sites for bainite transformation [ 54 , 55 ]. At the same time, the refined austenite grains hinder the growth of bainite laths, both the elongation and widening of bainite laths [ 25 , 56 ], and no obvious bainite laths are formed.  Fig. 14 (j)  shows that the BF of banded bainite in the non-recrystallized zone has a polygonal shape.

With the increase of annealing temperature and prolongation of time, the bainite fraction increases continuously. Therefore, further quantitative analysis of the bainite transformation process was carried out. The changes of bainite fraction and transformation rate in samples annealed for 90 s during isothermal 600 s at 380 °C, as shown in  Fig. 15 
                         (a) and (b). The fraction of bainite were approximately estimated by the change in linear thermal expansion coefficient (LTEC) because the LTEC of each phase in the steel is different [ 4 , 57 ]. With the increase of annealing temperature, the bainite fraction and transformation rate gradually increase, and the bainite fraction and transformation rate of CH-t steel are always higher than that of CH steel. With a difference of 0.39%/s, the maximum bainite transformation rate of 880-90-t is 1.04%/s, while that of 880-90 is 0.65%/s. The bainite transformation rate depends on the nucleation kinetics. The bainite transformation rate of the untransformed austenite of samples annealed at 860 °C, and 880 °C for 90 s will be counted. The research shows that if the orientation difference gradient from the point to the origin is greater than 2°/5 μm, it is bainite; otherwise, it is ferrite [ 36 ]. Through analysis, the orientation gradients of the two selected bainite grains are about 2°/μm and 1.8°/μm respectively, so we consider them to be bainite. Then, the bainite-austenite orientation analysis was performed. Previous studies have shown that the orientation relationship between bainite and austenite in multiphase steel is mainly K-S relationship and Nishiyama-Wassermann (N-W) relationship [ 30 , 63 , 64 ]. (d)–(f) are pole figures of retained austenite, and (g)–(i) are pole figures of bainite. The results show that there is not only K-S relationship between retained austenite and bainite, but also N-W relationship, and the N-W relationship between bainite and retained austenite in the non-recrystallized zone is relatively high.

sections.heading: Microstructures and mechanical properties
paragraphs: As mentioned above, recrystallization plays a decisive role in microstructure evolution. The initial purpose of inhibiting the recrystallization by increasing the batch annealing process is to improve the strength of CH steel with the simplest method and provide guidance for industrial production. With the exception of when it is annealed at 880 °C for 10 s, CH-t steel has a higher tensile strength than CH steel. Except when annealed at 780 °C for 90 s, there is little difference between the elongation of CH steel and CH-t steel. According to the mechanical properties in the longitudinal direction of cold-rolled CH steels presented in VDA 239-100, the samples in this study meet the mechanical properties requirements of high-strength grades CH1180 and CH1370 steel.

Recrystallization of CH-t steel is incompletely annealed at the low temperature of 780 °C, and the grains are refined. The deformation starts from the soft phase ferrite during tensile, but dislocation entanglement is not conducive to dislocation movement, resulting the strength is improved but not conducive to enhancing plasticity [ 65 ]. The main reasons why 780-10-t's tensile strength is not significantly greater than 780-10 are that it contains more undissolved cementite, less austenite transformation, and more ferrite fraction. When the annealing temperature is increased to 820 °C, the recrystallization fraction of CH-t steel increases, the dislocation strengthening effect caused by non-recrystallization weakens, the fraction of low angle grain boundaries decreases, and the degree of strength improvement decreases, mainly because grain refinement strengthening and precipitation strengthening. Compared with 820-10, 820-10-t has a higher ferrite content, and there is still a small amount of non-recrystallized ferrite, but the large-sized martensite/ferrite interface of 820-10 steel is more prone to stress concentration, resulting in a break [ 66 ]. In comparison to 820-90, 820-90-t has the higher fraction of hard phase bainite and martensite, and the higher strength.

When the annealing temperature rises to 860 °C and 880 °C, the strength improvement effect decreases, and the elongation tends to increase. After high-temperature annealing, the effect of non-recrystallization is weakened, the degree of recrystallization and austenitization is further increased, and the austenite grain size is enlarged. The larger proportion of bainite in the microstructure is beneficial to coordinate deformation and improve elongation compared with the larger fraction of massive martensite, so the elongation of 860-90-t is greater than that of 860-90. However, it lowers the difference between CH and CH-t steel and is not helpful for increasing strength. Compared with 880-10-t steel, the grains of 880-10 steel are obviously coarser, and a large amount of massive martensite is formed during the secondary quenching process. Although there is more ferrite, the strength is still high. 880-90 and 880-90-t have a higher degree of austenitization, and the larger driving force of bainite transformation, forming a large number of granular bainite containing small-sized M/A islands, which can hinder crack propagation, enhance the ability to coordinate deformation, and increase elongation [ 67 ]. As the annealing temperature increased, cementite dissolved, RA content also tended to increase. The content and stability of RA jointly control the TRIP effect. Several factors affect the stability of RA, one of which is carbon content. According to the literatures [ 68–70 ], RA with a lower carbon content (<0.6%) causes the RA to transform at low levels of strain and the higher carbon content (>1.8%) prevents the RA from martensite transformation. Although the amount of retained austenite in CH steel and CH-t steel is small, it can still exert a certain TRIP effect with appropriate carbon content. The hardness difference, fraction ratio, grain size, morphology, and distribution of soft/hard structures are crucial for CH steel [ 50 , 71 ]. In conclusion, without severe loss of plasticity, hindering recrystallization during the annealing process can increase the dislocation strengthening, grain refinement strengthening, and precipitation strengthening values of the test steel, and the strength can be significantly improved. However, with the increase of annealing temperature, recrystallization fraction increased gradually, and the increase in strength becomes less noticeable.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
(1) 
                            After the hot-rolled sheet was batch annealed at 580 °C for 12 h, the grain boundaries of the microstructure were blurred, the fraction of low angle grain boundaries decreased, and a large amount of cementite and nanoscale (Nb, Ti)C precipitated. The yield strength increased by 137 MPa, the tensile strength decreased by 171 MPa, and the hardness reduced by 10.4%. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            After batch annealing was processed,  A 
                               c1  and  A 
                               c1f  of the cold-rolled sheet increased,  A 
                               c3  decreased, and the austenite transformation process accelerated. Carbide hindered the recrystallization process during the annealing process, resulting in significant refining of the grains. When the annealing time was 10 s, BCC's grain refinement ranged from 9.5% to 24.6%. With the prolongation of the annealing time to 90 s, the difference between CH steel and CH-t steel gradually decreased, and the BCC's grain refinement ranged from 6.8% to 13.3%. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            The lower recrystallization promoted bainite transformation and provided more nucleation sites for bainite nucleation. Higher grain boundary nucleation and autocatalytic nucleation activation energy of CH-t steel improved bainite's fraction and transformation rate. The maximum bainite nucleation rate of untransformed austenite in 880-90-t steel was about 1.5 times that of untransformed austenite in 880-90 steel. The bainitic ferrite was mainly lathy in the recrystallized zone and polygonal in the non-recrystallized zone. Both a K-S and an N-W relationship between retained austenite and bainite, while the N-W relationship in the non-recrystallized zone was relatively higher. 
                         
                         
                            (4) 
                            In the base of no severe loss of plasticity, the dislocation, grain refinement, and precipitation strengthening values of the samples can be increased by hindering recrystallization, and the strength was significantly improved. However, as the annealing temperature rose, recrystallization fraction increased gradually, and the increase in strength became less noticeable. The samples have good mechanical properties and meet the mechanical property requirements of high-strength grades CH1180 and CH1370 steel.
